description:
Other teams will show you Earth's data. We'll make you hear it.

The Fourier Collective is a two-person team combining astrophysics research, audio synthesis, digital signal processing, and scientific visualization. We're building an interactive instrument that turns NASA Earth-observation data into sound while preserving its scientific meaning.

Rigor, curiosity, ambition.
summary: EarthSynth responds to the Earth Information Jukebox by allowing blind and low-vision users to explore NASA visualisations through sound. Values are extracted from NASA visualisation frames using published colour bars. Three layers may be played simultaneously or individually; these include ECCO2 ocean temperatures (SVS3912), GEOS-CF modelled nitrogen oxides globally (NO+NO2) (SVS5518) for July 1st 2024 and GEOS-FP modelled near surface winds (SVS5148) for October 30th 2026. Due to the different dates, it is not a simultaneous weather visualisation. The wind remains in image space. Each value dictates the relative amplitude of two constant pitches, 220 and 880 Hz. Real time FFTs are calculated for each carrier wave. This checks that the values recovered match those encoded. This does not confirm the accuracy of the NASA models. Gaps in data will result in silence. There is only one background piece of music and there is no independent measurement encoded in it. The interface provides keyboard controls, text values, optional screen reader announcements and reduced-motion support. The application is written in vanilla JavaScript using Web Audio and Canvas. Preprocessing was done in Python.
details:
EarthSynth plays NASA Earth imagery as music. You pick a dataset, pick a musical key, and press play. A scan line moves across the image and the chords change as it goes, but the number under the scan line rides in the tone color of the sound rather than in the notes, which leaves the melody free for us to write.

Every voice in the synth is built from two sine partials, one at 220 Hz and one at 880 Hz. Both are A naturals two octaves apart, so they stay in tune with whatever key the piece is in. The measured value sets how energy is split between them: we convert the value to a tilt in decibels using a linear function, then raise one partial by half the tilt and lower the other by half. Total energy stays constant, so loudness carries no information and cannot be mistaken for data. Because the rule is a fixed linear function, it also runs backwards. Record the output, take an FFT, sum the power in a few bins around each partial, and the ratio of the two gives you the tilt; put that through the inverse function and the original value comes back. The analysis window's gain appears in both bands, so it cancels in the ratio.

EarthSynth runs that FFT on its own output while the track plays and displays the difference between the recovered value and the true one. There is also a control labeled Break the encoder, which adds a deliberate offset to what is sounded while leaving the displayed target alone, and the residual jumps immediately. That is what proves the number on screen is being read from the audio rather than copied from the file. You can also export the track as a WAV and run your own analysis outside the browser.

The values themselves are inverted out of NASA's published frames. An offline Python script converts each pixel to OKLab, finds the nearest color on the published color bar, and reads off the corresponding value. Pixels too far from any color on the bar are rejected and drawn as a mask, so you can see exactly what was discarded. The shipped tracks come from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio: an ECCO2 ocean surface current visualization and a global nitrogen dioxide average for 2005. Not every image has a published scale, and tracks loaded without one are marked unanchored when they load, so the app makes no numeric claim about them; they still sound like something without pretending to be measurements.

The challenge asks for a tool that makes Earth data reachable by people who cannot read a chart, so we treated accessibility as the main requirement rather than a finishing touch. Every control is a native HTML element and works from the keyboard. A single live region announces the current reading, throttled so a screen reader is not flooded while the track plays. Every value shown in color is also shown as text, and the validation result carries a check or cross character so it never depends on color alone. The globe varies lightness rather than hue, which keeps it readable under the common forms of color blindness.

It is plain JavaScript as ES modules, with no framework and no build step. The Web Audio API drives the synthesis, and Canvas 2D draws the frames, the color bar, the trend graph, and the rotating globe, which is drawn pixel by pixel in JavaScript rather than with a 3D library. The frame inversion pipeline is an offline Python script. Tests run on Node's built-in test runner with jsdom for the page tests, 79 of them covering the encoder, the inverse, and the interface wiring.

What we spent the most time on was deciding what we were willing to claim. Mapping value to pitch would have been easier and would have sounded more dramatic, but nobody could have checked it, and a sonification nobody can audit is a picture with a soundtrack. So we built the audit first and wrote the music around it.
